_note: Master series of Edo-period monster encyclopedias — yokai illustrations that defined Japanese supernatural iconography
Sekien's second monster encyclopedia (1779) — 60 images of supernatural beings from literature and folklore, many Sekien's own inventions
Sekien's third monster encyclopedia (1781) — 52 images, expanding the yokai bestiary with creatures from Chinese sources and Sekien's imagination
Piranesi's Imaginary Prisons (1750–1761) — hallucinatory architectural etchings of impossible dungeons that anticipate Romantic and Surrealist dream logic
First edition of Piranesi's Prisons — looser, more dreamlike plates before his 1761 reworking darkened the shadows
Second edition of Piranesi's Prisons — heavily reworked with deeper shadow and more oppressive atmosphere, 14 plates
Hildegard von Bingen's Scivias (1151) — 35 illuminated visions of cosmic structure, divine fire, the Fall, and the heavenly city; Rupertsberg manuscript and copies
Full Hildegard von Bingen category — includes Scivias, Liber Vitae Meritorum, and related illuminated manuscript imagery
All illustrations from the 1863 sixth edition of Collin de Plancy's Dictionnaire Infernal — 69 demon portraits engraved by Louis Le Breton, the definitive visual catalog of demonology
Focused subcategory: 148 demon drawings — Astaroth, Bael, Behemoth, Belzébuth, Malphas, and 64 others from Le Breton's engravings

Ethiopian Orthodox church murals — angelic ceilings of Gondar, saints from Lalibela rock-hewn churches, bold flat color with large almond eyes; one of Christianity's oldest continuous artistic traditions
Ethiopian depictions of Saint George slaying the dragon — the patron saint of Ethiopia rendered in distinctive Gondar and Lalibela church painting style
Tibetan Buddhist protector deity — wrathful form of Avalokiteshvara; 91 images including thangkas from multiple traditions (two-armed, four-armed, six-armed, white Mahakala)
Yamantaka (Vajrabhairava) — 'Destroyer of Death', bull-headed wrathful form of Manjushri; Gelug school thangkas and sculpture; among the most fearsome wrathful deities in Vajrayana
Jacques Callot's complete etching output — includes the massive 1635 Temptation of Saint Anthony and his demonic fantasies; technically innovative use of the échoppe needle
Schongauer's c.1470 engraving — grotesque demons swarm the levitating saint; influenced Michelangelo, Dürer, and the entire tradition of supernatural engraving
Yoshitoshi's early ghost series (1865) — 26 of the projected 100 completed; yurei, demons, and spirit warriors from Japanese and Chinese legend
Yoshitoshi's New Forms of Thirty-Six Ghosts (1889–1892) — his final and greatest ghost series; technically brilliant woodblocks using burnishing, embossing, bokashi shading
Ukiyo-e depictions of tengu — the great bird-like mountain spirits of Japanese folklore; crow-headed and long-nosed variants across multiple artists
Ukiyo-e of kitsune fox spirits — shapeshifting supernatural foxes in Japanese art; includes the nine-tailed fox and Kuzunoha
Kawanabe Kyōsai's supernatural works — Hyakki Yako (Monster Parade), Jigoku-dayū (Hell Courtesan), demon scrolls; bridge between Edo and Meiji supernatural imagery
Persian and Turkic illustrated Miraj-nama manuscripts — the Prophet Muhammad's night journey through the heavens and hells; 14th–15th century Timurid masterpieces from Tabriz and Herat
Full category for Isra and Mi'raj iconography — Muhammad on Buraq ascending through the seven heavens; Persian, Turkish, and Mughal manuscript illuminations
19th-century illustrations of Norse myths — Odin, Thor, Valkyries, Ragnarok by artists including Rackham, Doré, and the Scandinavian Romantics
Painted works depicting Norse supernatural beings — Asgard, the World Tree, Norse gods and monsters from the Romantic and National Revival period
Rackham's 1911 illustrations for Wagner's Ring Cycle — brooding, naturalistic depictions of Norse-derived supernatural beings; Siegfried, the dragon Fafner, the Rhinemaidens
Goya's supernatural paintings — Witches' Sabbath (1798), Saturn Devouring His Son, the Black Paintings from Quinta del Sordo; the darkest supernatural vision of the Enlightenment
Multiple versions of Goya's Witches' Sabbath — the great He-Goat presiding over a coven; both the 1798 Osuna and 1820–23 Black Painting versions
Schongauer, Saint Anthony Tormented by Demons, c.1470–75 — the print that launched a tradition; Met holds a superb impression; Michelangelo copied it at age 13
Jacques Callot, Temptation of Saint Anthony — 336568 is an early state; 423476 is La Tentation de St. Antoine (1635), Callot's last and largest etching, a panorama of hell's armies
After Hieronymus Bosch, Temptation of Saint Anthony — engraving after Bosch's Lisbon triptych, preserving the 16th-century monster vocabulary
Met Mahakala thangkas — Protector of the Tent (Central Tibet), Tantric Protective Form (early Tibetan), Brahmarupa Mahakala, White Mahakala, four-armed Mahakala in tiger-skin skirt
Met, Yamantaka Destroyer of the God of Death — Tibetan thangka; the bull-headed deity of the Gelug school
Sultan Muhammad Nur, The Mi'raj or Night Flight of Muhammad on his Steed Buraq, Folio 3v from a Bustan of Sa'di, c.1525–35 (Bukhara/Herat) — the Prophet on the winged horse ascending to heaven
The Fabulous Creature Buraq — hybrid beast with a woman's face, horse's body, wings, and dragon tail; depicted without rider as an independent icon of the miraculous
Utagawa Kuniyoshi, Scene from a Ghost Story: The Okazaki Cat Demon — Edo-period woodblock print; the cat-ghost Okabe, one of Kuniyoshi's most celebrated supernatural images
Tsukioka Yoshitoshi supernatural prints — 73574: Spirit of Akugenta Yoshihira strikes Nanba Jirō at Nunobiki Waterfall; 72828: Fudō Myōō Threatening a Novice (wrathful Buddhist deity)
Ethiopian Double Diptych Icon Pendant, early 18th c. — four painted surfaces: Virgin with Christ flanked by archangels; portable sacred object of the Ethiopian Orthodox tradition
Ethiopian Icon Triptych of Ewosṭatewos and Eight Disciples — only known icon devoted to genealogy of an Ethiopian monastic order; Northern Highlands artist, Amhara tradition
Ethiopian Madonna and Child paintings — the distinctive flat, frontal style with archangels Michael and Gabriel as flanking guardians; Gondar and pre-Gondar periods
14th-century Tabriz Miraj-nama from Topkapi Saray (Hazine 2154) — the oldest surviving illustrated account of Muhammad's ascent; bold Ilkhanid style, angel-crowded heavens
Arthur Rackham's complete Wagner opera illustrations — Ring of the Nibelung (1910–11); Norse supernatural beings rendered in Rackham's distinctive pen-and-wash style
